newsitem.title: USA: Dole demands Clinton answer fundraising questions.
newsitem.headline: Dole demands Clinton answer fundraising questions.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole demanded on Monday that President Bill Clinton answer questions about his links to Asian businessmen and their contributions to Democratic party coffers.
Speaking to reporters in Kansas City, Dole joined other Republicans who have criticised donations to the Democrats from foreigners and highlighted the potential impact on Clinton's foreign policy.
"We're going to raise the questions every day until the president's properly responded," Dole said.

"Not some slip, slide and duck, Mr. President. Just answer the questions," the Republican said before boarding a plane for San Diego, where he and Clinton hold their second and final presidential debate on Wednesday.

Dole did not specifically say whether he would bring up the foreign donations in the San Diego debate, but in a rally earlier in Kansas City he promised to get tougher with Clinton than he was in their first face-off Oct. 6.

Clinton's ties to Indonesian James Riady have been fiercely attacked by Republicans in recent days, who suspect Riady's influence is behind big contributions to the Democratic Party from individuals with links to an Indonesian financial conglomerate, the Lippo Group.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Sunday investigations were "unavoidable" into an Indonesian couple's $425,000 contribution to the Democratic Party, and another donation from a South Korean company that the party returned after media queries about it.
When Dole was first asked about the matter on Monday by reporters after speaking to the rally in Kansas City, he indicated he might wait until Tuesday to comment.
But later, at the airport, Dole noted his campaign had issued a press release raising questions about the foreign donations, and said the president should respond "immediately."

"There are a whole lot of problems here that have been raised," Dole said. "Taking money from a foreign nation. They gave it back when somebody caught them, but why did they do it? Why did he (Clinton) meet with these people?"

"Did it have any impact on the policies in East Timor?" he continued, referring to the former Portuguese colony which was incorporated into Indonesia in 1976 and where human rights questions have been raised.
"They do raise serious questions about campaign contributions, about influencing U.S. foreign policy," Dole said.

During the Kansas City rally, attended by about 1,000 people, Dole said about 30 members of Clinton's administration "are already gone -- they are in jail or they are indicted or they are out of there."
"Then he talks about an ethical administration," Dole said. "Well, he does not have an ethical administration and we're going to go after him on that on Wednesday night."

Dole recalled Democratic President Harry Truman, from nearby Independence, Missouri, used to say, "The buck stops here," but he added his own twist: "Bill Clinton says the buck doesn't stop anywhere. It just keeps on going."

In Albuquerque, New Mexico, where Clinton was preparing for the debate, the president dodged questions about the foreign donations. "It's election time," was Clinton's sole response. But that was before Dole spoke on the issue.
Later, after Dole's comments, Clinton's campaign press secretary Joe Lockhart issued a statement saying Dole had obviously rejected advice that he keep clear of personal attacks.

"In this moment of desperation, it's clear that Senator Dole has decided to ignore the advice of his own running mate Jack Kemp, Colin Powell and several former colleagues from the Senate," Lockhart said.
